title: SeDebugPrivilege Enabled in a Windows Process Token
exclusions: Reports Windows Security Event ID 4703 when `EnabledPrivilegeList` explicitly contains `SeDebugPrivilege`. It does not report privileges merely assigned at logon (4672), a privileged service/object attempt (4673/4674), user-right policy assignment/removal (4704/4705), disabled privileges, token theft/duplication, process injection, credential access, or successful privilege escalation. Event 4703 records a token privilege being enabled or disabled; this rule selects enabled SeDebugPrivilege only. Microsoft documents potentially very high 4703 volume when applications dynamically adjust tokens, and the required audit subcategory is off by default in current guidance. The five-minute cadence, five-minute allowance, one-event trigger, severity, retention, and exceptions are deployment choices. The rule performs no process termination, token change, account disable, isolation, or compliance attestation.
evidence: After deployment, retain the approved `Audit Token Right Adjustment` Success policy scope and effective-policy evidence; Security XML input and Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows version; expected endpoint/process/token-adjustment baseline; source/field/volume health; `windows_sedebug_privilege_enabled` saved-search definition/ACL/schedule/dispatch; every result and raw 4703 XML; correlated 4688/Sysmon/EDR process, logon, target-process, handle/API, software/change, and disposition evidence; exact bounded exception; and dated positive, disabled-list, wrong-event, boundary, duplicate, delayed, field-loss, volume, and recovery tests. This documentation-only review changed no audit policy or token and executed no process, event, search, alert, dashboard, or response.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated index and fixed dispatch slice, replay authentic-shaped Security XML EventCode 4703 with Provider_Name `Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing`, EnabledPrivilegeList `SeDebugPrivilege`, ProcessName `C:\Lab\uc12123-test.exe`, ProcessId `0x570`, distinct Computer, SubjectUserName/DomainName/Sid/LogonId, TargetUserName/DomainName/Sid/LogonId, EventRecordID, `_time`, and `_indextime`. Expect exactly one `sedebug_privilege_enabled` row, decimal process ID 1392, preserved subject/target identities, and `use_case=UC-1.2.123`. Repeat with multiple enabled privileges including SeDebugPrivilege and expect one event row.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Replay EventCode 4703 with SeDebugPrivilege only in DisabledPrivilegeList, EnabledPrivilegeList containing `SeBackupPrivilege` or a lookalike `MySeDebugPrivilegeSuffix`, EventCodes 4672/4673/4674/4704 from the correct Security source, EventCode 4703 from a wrong provider/source/type, and an out-of-window event; expect zero rows. Replay a missing ProcessName or target identity and expect a retained row with `unknown` plus a field-quality finding. Prove an exact unexpired endpoint/process/hash/target/software exception suppresses delivery only after the base event; expired, path-only, actor-only, wildcard, or source-health exceptions must not hide evidence.

dataSources: Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing Event ID 4703 from the local Security log after `Audit Token Right Adjustment` (documented on the 4703 page under Audit Authorization Policy Change) Success is enabled, collected as XML to deployment-chosen `index=windows`, `source=XmlWinEventLog:Security`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`. Required fields are `_time`, `_indextime`, `Computer`/`host`, provider, `EventCode`, `EventRecordID`, `SubjectUserSid`, `SubjectUserName`, `SubjectDomainName`, `SubjectLogonId`, `TargetUserSid`, `TargetUserName`, `TargetDomainName`, `TargetLogonId`, `ProcessName`, `ProcessId`, `EnabledPrivilegeList`, and `DisabledPrivilegeList`.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) 10.0.1 or a later compatible release supplies XML Security collection and Event ID 4703 process/account extraction. A deployment app supplies the high-volume-safe input policy, source/volume health, raw saved search, process baseline, dashboard, fixtures, and exact exception lookup. No premium Splunk app is required.
spl:
index=windows sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog source="XmlWinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4703 earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval provider=lower(trim(coalesce(Provider_Name,SourceName,"unknown"))), endpoint=lower(trim(coalesce(Computer,dest,host))), enabled_privileges=trim(coalesce(EnabledPrivilegeList,"")), disabled_privileges=trim(coalesce(DisabledPrivilegeList,"")), process_path=coalesce(ProcessName,process_path,process,"unknown"), process_id_raw=coalesce(ProcessId,process_id,"unknown"), subject_user=coalesce(SubjectUserName,src_user_name,"unknown"), subject_domain=coalesce(SubjectDomainName,"unknown"), subject_sid=coalesce(SubjectUserSid,"unknown"), subject_logon_id=coalesce(SubjectLogonId,"unknown"), target_user=coalesce(TargetUserName,user_name,"unknown"), target_domain=coalesce(TargetDomainName,"unknown"), target_sid=coalesce(TargetUserSid,object_id,"unknown"), target_logon_id=coalesce(TargetLogonId,"unknown"), event_record_id=coalesce(EventRecordID,RecordNumber,"unknown")
| where provider="microsoft-windows-security-auditing" AND len(endpoint)>0 AND match(enabled_privileges,"(?i)(^|\\s)SeDebugPrivilege(\\s|$)")
| eval process_id_decimal=if(match(process_id_raw,"(?i)^0x"),tonumber(replace(process_id_raw,"(?i)^0x",""),16),tonumber(process_id_raw)), action="sedebug_privilege_enabled", event_time=strftime(_time,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), indexed_time=strftime(_indextime,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), use_case="UC-1.2.123"
| table _time event_time indexed_time endpoint action process_path process_id_raw process_id_decimal enabled_privileges disabled_privileges subject_user subject_domain subject_sid subject_logon_id target_user target_domain target_sid target_logon_id event_record_id source sourcetype use_case
| sort 0 -_time endpoint process_path target_user
description: Detects each Windows Security Event ID 4703 whose enabled-privilege list contains the exact SeDebugPrivilege token right during the completed dispatch slice. Results preserve the adjusting process/PID, requesting subject, target token identity/logon, enabled and disabled lists, event identity, and event/index times without asserting token theft or successful escalation.
value: SeDebugPrivilege can give a process extensive access to other processes and critical operating-system components, so an unexpected token enablement warrants rapid ownership and lineage review. Exact event/list matching accelerates correlation with process, handle, target, and change evidence while avoiding the false claim that generic sensitive-privilege service calls prove token manipulation.
implementation: Risk-assess and selectively enable `Audit Token Right Adjustment` Success because Microsoft classifies Event ID 4703 volume as high and documents noisy dynamic adjustments. Collect Security XML with Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows 10.0.1, validate EnabledPrivilegeList/process/subject/target fields, and save `windows_sedebug_privilege_enabled`. Run every five minutes over the preceding complete slice after five minutes of measured ingestion allowance; trigger on each result, then compare exact process/hash, token target, software, endpoint role, and change approval before escalation.
visualization: Dashboard `Windows — SeDebugPrivilege Token Enablement`: lead with audit-policy/source coverage, Event ID 4703 rate, volume/cardinality guardrails, field quality, and endpoints excluded from collection. Show newest events by endpoint, process/path/hash enrichment, subject and target token/logon, enabled/disabled lists, asset role/owner, baseline/exception, and disposition; add process/target prevalence, post-enable process-access/activity correlation, and raw XML drilldown. Never label the event credential dumping, injection, or SYSTEM escalation without corroboration.
dataModelAcceleration: Not used by the primary detector. The Windows add-on provides Change/account/process aliases for 4703, but generic Change or Authentication summaries do not guarantee the exact EnabledPrivilegeList versus DisabledPrivilegeList distinction, target token logon, raw process ID, provider/source, EventRecordID, and raw XML. A normalized analytic may be introduced only after parity and volume tests; the raw event remains authoritative.

knownFalsePositives:
A returned row is a genuine Event ID 4703 SeDebugPrivilege enablement; the false positive is treating every dynamic token adjustment as malicious token theft or escalation.

1. **Microsoft Configuration Manager/WMI inventory activity** — Microsoft explicitly documents Configuration Manager WMI queries as a potentially high-volume 4703 source commonly shown as `svchost.exe`. Verify exact endpoint role, service/process path and hash, target token, Configuration Manager client/version/job, WMI activity, cadence, and owner. Do not globally suppress svchost or all managed endpoints.

2. **Endpoint security, EDR, antivirus, anti-cheat, or diagnostics agent** — Security/diagnostic products may enable debug privilege for inspection. Require signed package/hash/version, service identity, target token/process behavior, vendor documentation, deployment inventory, and change record. Publisher/path alone is insufficient.

3. **Approved debugger, profiler, crash dump, or performance tool** — Administrators/developers may use WinDbg, ProcDump, Visual Studio, profiler, or support utilities. Match exact binary/hash, operator/logon, target process, ticket, endpoint class, exclusive UTC window, and evidence of intended diagnostics.

4. **Backup, restore, migration, or forensic acquisition software** — Privileged tools can adjust tokens during protected data/process access. Confirm signed tool/version, job/case ID, service account, endpoint set, target, schedule, owner, and bounded run. A backup window alone must not exempt unrelated processes.

5. **Operating-system service behavior** — Qualified Windows services may legitimately enable sensitive privileges. Establish a versioned per-build tuple of exact process hash/path, subject/target, enabled-list, service/function context, endpoint role, and prevalence. Never hard-code `lsass`, `services`, or `svchost` as universally safe.

6. **Authorized red-team or detection control** — Match exercise ID, named operator, exact endpoint/process/hash/target, exclusive time, expected follow-on process-access behavior, and cleanup. Preserve raw event and alert evidence.

7. **Duplicate direct/WEC collection or replay** — Compare Computer, channel, EventRecordID, raw hash, and `_indextime`. Repair routing/checkpoint state rather than suppressing by process or privilege.

**Safe notification suppression:** apply lookup windows_sedebug_token_exceptions.csv after the base row, keyed by exact lowercase endpoint or governed asset group, full process path and hash/signer, subject and target SID/logon context, software/version/job identifier, numeric `valid_from`/exclusive `valid_until`, owner, approver, ticket, and reason. Reject path-only, actor-only, broad Microsoft/System32, wildcard, open-ended, unknown-process, and source-health exceptions. Preserve the original result and matched exception.
hardware: Windows endpoints/servers where Audit Token Right Adjustment Success is deliberately enabled and Security XML is collected. Microsoft classifies this event stream as high volume and default No Auditing in current advanced-audit guidance; capacity qualification and scoped deployment are prerequisites.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against primary Microsoft Event ID 4703, Audit Token Right Adjusted, 4673/4674 distinction, current Splunk Windows add-on and Security Content, and MITRE ATT&CK behavior-chain guidance; no audit-policy deployment, token adjustment, event generation, SPL/CIM execution, volume test, process baseline, fixture replay, exception, alert, dashboard, response, or Microsoft/Splunk/Windows-security SME runtime sign-off

cost.search_load_notes: The saved search itself filters one Event ID and exact privilege over five minutes, but Microsoft classifies Audit Token Right Adjustment as high volume and warns dynamic applications can generate many 4703 events. Endpoint Security-log/index/storage capacity and cardinality must be measured before broad enablement.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and corrected event contract

Assign Windows security/audit-policy, endpoint engineering, Splunk collection/content/capacity, application owners, incident response, and privacy roles. Inventory high-value endpoints, Windows build, Security-log sizing, direct versus WEF/WEC path, software known to adjust token rights, endpoint role, and owners. Qualify Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows 10.0.1 with the exact forwarder/indexer/search tier and Splunk release.

Use the event that matches the behavior. Microsoft says 4703 is generated when token privileges are enabled or disabled for a specific account token and exposes EnabledPrivilegeList/DisabledPrivilegeList plus process and target token. By contrast, 4673 records an attempt to perform a privileged system-service operation and 4674 an operation attempted on a privileged object. Those events can support investigation but do not say a process enabled SeDebugPrivilege in its token. This UC therefore replaces the old 4673/4674 “token manipulation” claim with exact 4703 enabled-right evidence.

SeDebugPrivilege allows powerful inspection/adjustment of other processes and critical system components, but enabling it is not proof it was used for token theft, injection, dumping, or escalation. MITRE recommends a behavior chain including token-related APIs/commands, a process under changed security context, lineage anomalies, and follow-on behavior. Preserve 4703 as one fact in that chain.

## Step 1 — Risk-assess and configure high-volume auditing

Microsoft's current advanced-audit guidance identifies **Audit Token Right Adjustment**, Event ID 4703, as high volume and default **No Auditing**; the older event page places it under Audit Authorization Policy Change. Determine the exact policy label/GUID for each supported Windows build and management system, document the naming discrepancy, and verify with effective audit-policy output. Enable Success only on a staged high-value cohort after sizing. The subcategory has no Failure events.

Canary on representative servers/workstations for at least a business cycle. Measure events/second, Security log wrap time, endpoint CPU/I/O, WEF throughput, forwarder queues, index GB/day, process/target cardinality, and Configuration Manager/WMI bursts. Establish stop/rollback thresholds before expansion. Do not enable broad 4703 auditing merely because this catalogue marks the use case critical.

Collect Security XML through an app-owned stanza:

```ini
[WinEventLog://Security]
disabled = 0
renderXml = true
index = windows
checkpointInterval = 5
```

Keep `source=XmlWinEventLog:Security` and `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`; do not edit add-on `default`. For WEF/WEC, preserve originating Computer, secure the subscription, size collector logs, measure latency, and prevent duplicate local/collector collection. Restrict token/account/process evidence to appropriate roles.

## Step 2 — Verify fields and independent source health

Inspect raw 4703 XML from representative legitimate adjustments. Verify provider, Computer, Subject SID/name/domain/logon, Target SID/name/domain/logon, ProcessName, hexadecimal ProcessId, EnabledPrivilegeList, DisabledPrivilegeList, EventRecordID, event version, keywords, event time, and index time. Confirm add-on aliases without replacing raw meanings. The SPL's exact whitespace-boundary match prevents a substring lookalike from firing.

Maintain expected audit-policy/source inventory. Health searches must detect policy disabled/drifted, no Security events, unexpectedly zero or runaway 4703 rate, Security-log overwrite/drop, wrong source/type/provider, missing process/target/lists, direct/WEC duplication, latency/clock skew, forwarder/collector queues, add-on drift, and cardinality spikes. Route source/volume failures separately and retain capacity telemetry. No SeDebug events is not a heartbeat.

Build a baseline from exact endpoint role, process path/hash/signer, subject and target SID/logon, full enabled-list, software/version/job, service/parent, cadence, and prevalence. A filename or System32 location is not sufficient because trusted binaries can be abused or replaced. Do not filter at ingestion until the security owner has proved a stable, necessary, reversible rule that preserves source health.

## Step 3 — Save, schedule, and understand the search

Save the sidecar SPL as `windows_sedebug_privilege_enabled`. Schedule every five minutes with `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m`, evaluating one completed five-minute slice after a fixed five-minute indexing allowance. Measure p99 direct/WEC delay and update schedule plus controls if inadequate. Trigger on every result; group delivery only on exact endpoint, process path/hash enrichment, target logon/SID, EventRecordID, and bounded time.

The base clause fixes Security XML, EventCode 4703, and dispatch bounds. Provider validation avoids number collisions. Coalescing retains documented raw fields/add-on aliases and uses `unknown` rather than silently dropping incomplete evidence. `match` selects SeDebugPrivilege only from EnabledPrivilegeList with whitespace boundaries; DisabledPrivilegeList alone cannot fire. ProcessId is preserved raw and converted from hexadecimal when possible. Output keeps subject (requesting context) distinct from target token identity.

Do not restore the old blanket exclusion for lsass/services/svchost/csrss/wininit/smss. Microsoft recommends comparison with a predefined expected process, not universal trust, and specifically documents svchost-backed Configuration Manager noise that should be qualified. Baseline/exception after base result generation. Do not use Authentication-model counts: this event is a token-right adjustment, not an authentication transaction.

## Step 4 — Validate event, boundaries, scale, and exceptions

Use authentic-shaped XML from qualified Windows/add-on versions and absolute dispatch times. Run both control scenarios. Add EnabledPrivilegeList cases with SeDebug alone, first/middle/last among multiple rights, varied whitespace, case variation, Disabled-only, lookalike suffix/prefix, empty process/target, hexadecimal/decimal/malformed PID, Unicode identities, and multiple rapid events. Add wrong provider/source/type/index, IDs 4672/4673/4674/4704/4705, and exact earliest/latest boundaries.

In a disposable lab only, use a reviewed benign test harness or approved debugger that calls the supported token-adjustment API to enable SeDebugPrivilege under a controlled account. Capture 4703 and compare Event Viewer **Details > XML View**, raw Splunk event, search row, process hash/signature, subject/target token, and process creation. Do not deploy exploit code, target credential processes, or adjust production tokens solely for testing.

Run load tests using representative Configuration Manager/WMI and endpoint-security workloads. Verify Security-log retention, WEC/forwarder/index queues, search runtime, result cardinality, dashboard limits, and alert throttling without hiding distinct records. Test policy disable/restore and recovery. Test exact exception matching, changed hash/target/version, expiry boundary, malformed rows, wildcard rejection, retained base evidence, and source-health independence. Keep draft until policy, capacity, fields, baseline, fixtures, alert, dashboard, exceptions, and response are accepted.

## Step 5 — Investigate as a behavior chain

Alert text should say `SeDebugPrivilege enabled in process token`, not `privilege escalation confirmed`. Include endpoint/role, process path/PID/hash/signer/parent enrichment, subject and target SID/name/domain/logon, full enabled/disabled lists, event/index times, record ID, software/job/change context, baseline/exception, and runbook.

Responder sequence:
1. Verify raw Security XML, provider/EventCode, EnabledPrivilegeList, process/target identity, times, record ID, source health, and duplicate state.
2. Correlate ProcessId/time with 4688 or Sysmon Event ID 1, resolving PID reuse via creation time/GUID; collect parent, command line, signer/hash, service/task, file provenance, user/session, and endpoint role.
3. Resolve SubjectLogonId and TargetLogonId against 4624 and token/account context. Determine why the process adjusted the target token and whether expected software owns it.
4. Correlate Sysmon Event ID 10/EDR process-access and handle telemetry, API/behavior detections, target process, memory access, child processes under changed context, credential access, network activity, and security-product findings.
5. Compare exact tuple with Configuration Manager, EDR, debugger/profiler, backup/forensic job, maintenance ticket, and baseline. Validate publisher and hash, not filename alone.
6. If suspicious, follow approved endpoint containment/evidence procedures. If authorized, document version/job/target and add only a bounded exception.
7. Confirm process/software disposition, no unexpected recurrence/follow-on activity, policy/source health, exception expiry, and retained evidence.

Never kill a process, disable an account, revoke rights, or isolate automatically from 4703 alone. Security, backup, management, or diagnostic software can depend on this right. Review baselines/exceptions after Windows, Configuration Manager, EDR, backup, debugger, audit-policy, WEC, or add-on changes.

## Step 6 — Troubleshoot product-specific failures

- **No 4703:** verify OS support, exact Audit Token Right Adjustment/Authorization Policy Change effective setting, Security log, source input, WEC/forwarder queues, index/RBAC, and dispatch time. Default may be No Auditing.
- **Volume overwhelms Security/WEC:** identify exact process/target/software tuples, validate Microsoft-documented dynamic adjusters, resize/limit policy scope, or disable per approved rollback. Do not allow log loss.
- **SeDebug appears only in DisabledPrivilegeList:** expected negative for this UC. Build a separate audit view if disablement matters; do not relabel it enabled.
- **ProcessName/target null:** inspect raw EventData, event version, XML rendering, add-on extraction placement/version, and conflicting props/transforms. Retain quality finding.
- **PID correlation finds wrong process:** ProcessId can be hexadecimal and reused. Use process creation time/GUID, endpoint, and narrow time; do not join PID across long windows.
- **svchost flood:** confirm Configuration Manager/WMI client, service hosting, target token, version/job/cadence, and Microsoft-described pattern before a narrow exception. Never exclude all svchost.
- **4673/4674 exists but 4703 does not:** those events mean privileged service/object attempts, not necessarily a token-right enablement. Investigate under their own semantics and verify 4703 policy.
- **Duplicate events:** compare Computer/channel/EventRecordID/raw hash/index time and direct/WEC/checkpoint routes. Repair collection rather than broad deduplication.
- **CIM differs from raw:** inspect add-on eventtypes/tags/aliases and acceleration. Keep raw EnabledPrivilegeList semantics authoritative.
grandmaExplanation: We watch when a Windows program turns on a powerful debugging right that can inspect other programs. Many management and security tools use it legitimately, so the team checks the exact program and target before deciding it is dangerous.
